fields.sections.0.exchanges.0.con.words: Dillahunty argues that Philemon is a personal exception, while repeated New Testament obedience commands and silence about abolition defeat the claimed anti-slavery trajectory.
fields.sections.0.exchanges.0.con.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty directly answers the abolitionist trajectory by distinguishing Paul’s personal plea for Onesimus from institutional condemnation and citing four epistles that command slave obedience, even to cruel masters. Principal limitation: Saying Philemon has nothing relevant to slavery is too categorical, since receiving Onesimus as a brother may exert relational pressure without expressly declaring slaveholding immoral. Live burden: He must show why that fraternal language and its context fail to undermine slave status, while defending his reading of the obedience passages beyond their bare presence and several ancillary moral claims. Locked score: The fixed 87 reflects a highly responsive, textually specific rebuttal, while contextual support and charitable calibration remain weaker than its direct engagement with the affirmative’s strongest claimed canonical trajectory.
